title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied and applied in higher education, with particular attention to how publications have developed over time, what conceptualisations and ethical issues appear in the literature, and what kinds of AI applications are being used. The authors conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2007 and November 2018, screening 2,656 records and including 146 articles in the final synthesis.

The review is not an intervention study of one tool, but a mapping of AI applications in higher education. It organises the literature into four application areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The paper also distinguishes learner-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing uses, and notes that most studies rely on quantitative methods, often machine learning, with a strong emphasis on prediction and automation.

The reviewed studies are mostly situated in higher education, especially undergraduate contexts, and cover both academic support services and institutional/administrative services. The authors conclude that AI in higher education is growing quickly, but the field shows limited critical reflection on ethical challenges, weak engagement with pedagogical theory, and relatively little attention to educators' roles. They argue for more work on ethical governance, teacher-facing applications, and educationally grounded implementation of AI.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it is not a primary impact study and does not test an intervention experimentally. It synthesizes descriptive and empirical studies with largely quantitative but heterogeneous methods, so it provides useful mapping evidence rather than causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has indirect relevance to K-12 scientific reasoning and inquiry because it is focused on higher education rather than school science. It offers a broad taxonomy of AI use cases, but no direct evidence of impact on K-12 learners, so the practical impact for the requested topic is limited and unclear.
